title.en: An opinion piece for the school magazine
title.es: Artículo de opinión para la revista escolar

es: Redactar un artículo de opinión para la revista escolar con tesis, dos argumentos, concesión, referencia interna y cierre, y documentar una revisión.

teaching.en: An opinion piece in the school magazine opens with its thesis: I will argue that pupils deserve a say in the rules.
teaching.es: Un artículo de opinión de la revista escolar abre con su tesis: defenderé que los alumnos merecen voz y voto en las normas.
teaching.explanationEs: I will argue that + oración anuncia la tesis; have a say in = tener voz y voto en.
segments: An opinion piece in the school magazine opens with its thesis:
I will argue that pupils deserve a say in the rules.
teaching.audioText: An opinion piece in the school magazine opens with its thesis: I will argue that pupils deserve a say in the rules.

teaching.en: I concede that pupils may not always choose wisely, but they respect the rules that they helped to write.
teaching.es: Admito que los alumnos no siempre eligen con acierto, pero respetan las normas que ayudaron a escribir.
teaching.explanationEs: Concede that + oración reconoce un punto antes de responderlo.
segments: I concede that pupils may not always choose wisely, but
they respect the rules that they helped to write.
teaching.audioText: I concede that pupils may not always choose wisely, but they respect the rules that they helped to write.

teaching.en: A writer may take issue with a counterargument, but answering it fairly makes the piece more convincing, not weaker.
teaching.es: Un autor puede discrepar de un contraargumento, pero responderlo con justicia hace el texto más convincente, no más débil.
teaching.explanationEs: Take issue with + sustantivo = discrepar de algo.
segments: A writer may take issue with a counterargument, but answering
it fairly makes the piece more convincing, not weaker.
teaching.audioText: A writer may take issue with a counterargument, but answering it fairly makes the piece more convincing, not weaker.

teaching.en: To persuade readers, build a compelling case with two clear reasons rather than five weak ones.
teaching.es: Para persuadir a los lectores, construye un argumento convincente con dos razones claras en lugar de cinco débiles.
teaching.explanationEs: Persuade + persona: persuade readers, no persuade to readers.
segments: To persuade readers, build a compelling case with
two clear reasons rather than five weak ones.
teaching.audioText: To persuade readers, build a compelling case with two clear reasons rather than five weak ones.

teaching.en: As mentioned above, rules that nobody explains are rarely followed, so a clear reason will persuade more readers than a threat.
teaching.es: Como se mencionó arriba, las normas que nadie explica rara vez se cumplen, así que una razón clara persuadirá a más lectores que una amenaza.
teaching.explanationEs: As mentioned above es una referencia interna: remite a lo ya dicho.
segments: As mentioned above, rules that nobody explains are rarely followed, so
a clear reason will persuade more readers than a threat.
teaching.audioText: As mentioned above, rules that nobody explains are rarely followed, so a clear reason will persuade more readers than a threat.

teaching.en: I revised my draft twice, cutting two repeated phrases and ending with one example to drive the point home.
teaching.es: Revisé mi borrador dos veces, recortando dos frases repetidas y terminando con un ejemplo para dejar clara la idea.
teaching.explanationEs: Drive the point home = insistir hasta que la idea quede clara.

prompt.es: ¿Qué frase expresa la tesis del artículo?

choices.text: The rules change every term, and nobody ever asks the pupils.
Some teachers disagree with this, which is perfectly understandable.
Pupils should have a say in the rules.

feedback.es: La tesis llega tras «I will argue that»; las otras frases describen un problema y admiten una objeción.

hint.es: Busca la postura que el autor anuncia con I will argue that.

origin.text: Every term the rules change, and nobody asks us. I will argue that pupils should have a say in the rules they live by. Some teachers disagree, which is understandable.

prompt.es: Completa: «Admito que quizá no siempre elijan con acierto.»

feedback.es: Concede that introduce un punto que el autor reconoce antes de responderlo con nevertheless.

hint.es: Verbo de la familia de concession.

origin.text: Pupils can make mistakes, and I ___ that they may not always choose wisely. Nevertheless, they respect the rules they helped to write.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Como se mencionó arriba, las normas sin explicación rara vez se cumplen.»

answer.text: As mentioned above rules without explanation are rarely followed
accepted: As mentioned above rules without explanation are rarely followed
Rules without explanation are rarely followed as mentioned above

feedback.es: As mentioned above remite a una idea ya expuesta y deja el resto de la frase intacta.

hint.es: La referencia interna abre la frase.

prompt.es: ¿Qué hace el autor con la objeción de «some»?

choices.text: He accepts part of it and adjusts his thesis accordingly.
He states it and answers it with a concrete example.
He answers it with a general principle but gives no example.
He uses it as the conclusion of his piece.

feedback.es: Enuncia la objeción («Some will say…»), discrepa («I take issue with…») y la rebate con el ejemplo de la política de celulares.

origin.text: Some will say that pupils cannot be trusted with rules. I take issue with that view. When pupils helped to write the phone policy last year, complaints fell by half, because people follow rules that they understand.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué aprendió la autora de la editora.

choices.text: A concession should be removed, because it weakens the thesis.
A draft should never be read aloud before it is revised.
A concession needs a reply, or the critic wins.
An editor should answer the objections, not the writer.

feedback.es: La editora le explica que conceder sin responder deja al lector donde lo dejó el crítico; con la respuesta, el texto queda completo.

origin.audio: Our magazine editor read my draft aloud and stopped after the third paragraph. You concede the main objection, she said, and then you never answer it. I had thought that admitting the point was enough. She explained that a concession without a reply leaves the reader exactly where the critic left him. I wrote two sentences of reply, and the piece suddenly felt finished.

prompt.es: Relaciona cada frase con la parte del artículo que representa.

pairs: I will argue that pupils deserve a say.
I concede that some rules are necessary.

feedback.es: Cada frase cumple una función: tesis, concesión, referencia interna o revisión.

pairs: I will argue that pupils deserve a say.
I concede that some rules are necessary.

prompt.es: ¿Qué actitud adopta el autor ante el riesgo de que elijan una norma poco sensata?

choices.text: He admits the risk, but thinks teachers would choose more wisely.
He thinks the risk decisive, so pupils should not be consulted.
He dismisses the risk, because a silly rule harms nobody in practice.
He admits the risk, yet thinks ignored rules do more harm.

feedback.es: Concede el riesgo («Admittedly») pero lo compara con el daño de una norma que nadie respeta: una concesión con refutación.

origin.text: Every September the school publishes a new list of rules, and every September most of us read it once and forget it. I will argue that this happens not because we are lazy, but because we were never asked. Rules that pupils help to write are followed more willingly, because people defend what they have built. Admittedly, a pupil council may choose a silly rule. Nevertheless, a silly rule can be changed next term, whereas a rule that nobody respects protects no one. In conclusion, the school should give us a say, and this magazine should keep asking for it.

prompt.es: ¿A qué se refiere «this» en la segunda frase del texto?

choices.text: To the habit of reading the list once and forgetting it.
To the decision to publish a new list of rules every September.
To the pupils' refusal to be asked about the rules at all.
To the change in the rules that the school introduced this year.

feedback.es: «This» retoma lo dicho justo antes: la costumbre de leer la lista una vez y olvidarla.

prompt.es: Completa: «Un contraargumento respondido con justicia hace el texto más convincente.»

feedback.es: Un counterargument respondido con justicia muestra al lector que el autor ha considerado el otro lado.

origin.text: The writer states the main objection and then gives a fair reply. A ___ answered fairly makes a piece sound more convincing, not weaker.

prompt.es: Redacta el artículo de opinión con revisión documentada (250–310 palabras).

answer.text: I will argue that the school should not ban phones at break, because a ban solves the wrong problem. First, pupils use their phones to talk to friends who are in other classes, and this contact is the only chance they have to do so. Second, a ban teaches pupils to hide their phones instead of using them well. Last term, for example, my class agreed on a simple rule and complaints fell by half. Admittedly, some pupils spend the whole break looking at a screen. Nevertheless, this is a problem of habits, not of phones, and, as mentioned above, a rule that pupils help to write is easier to respect. Some teachers take issue with this view, but a sensible alternative would be phone-free zones, which persuade without pushing anybody. I also believe that the school should trust us more, because trust is the best way to teach responsibility. In conclusion, the school should give us a say and trust us to use our phones well. Revision: I cut two repeated phrases and replaced due to the fact that with because.
accepted: I will argue that the school should not ban phones at break, because a ban solves the wrong problem. First, pupils use their phones to talk to friends who are in other classes, and this contact is the only chance they have to do so. Second, a ban teaches pupils to hide their phones instead of using them well. Last term, for example, my class agreed on a simple rule and complaints fell by half. Admittedly, some pupils spend the whole break looking at a screen. Nevertheless, this is a problem of habits, not of phones, and, as mentioned above, a rule that pupils help to write is easier to respect. Some teachers take issue with this view, but a sensible alternative would be phone-free zones, which persuade without pushing anybody. I also believe that the school should trust us more, because trust is the best way to teach responsibility. In conclusion, the school should give us a say and trust us to use our phones well. Revision: I cut two repeated phrases and replaced due to the fact that with because.

In my opinion, the school should not take phones away at break, because a ban would hurt pupils who use them sensibly. First, many of us talk to friends from other classes, and this is often our only chance to do so. Second, a strict rule would teach us to hide our phones rather than to control them. Last year, for instance, our class made its own rule, and arguments about phones almost disappeared. It is true that some pupils stare at a screen for the whole break. Even so, this is a question of habits, and, as noted above, rules that pupils help to write are easier to respect. A reasonable alternative would be quiet zones, where phones are allowed only for messages. Some teachers take issue with this view, but I think it is fair to ask them for trust. In short, pupils deserve a say in this decision, and the magazine should keep asking for it. Revision: I trimmed two long sentences and removed a repeated example.

feedback.es: Un artículo completo tiene tesis, dos argumentos, concesión con respuesta, referencia interna, cierre y una revisión documentada.

origin.text: Tema: el colegio quiere prohibir los celulares en los recreos. Escribe un artículo de opinión para la revista escolar: tesis, dos argumentos, una concesión con su respuesta, una referencia interna y un cierre. Termina con una nota de revisión que diga qué has cambiado (Revision: I cut…).

prompt.es: ¿Qué opina Carlos de los dos argumentos de Sara?

choices.text: The second is clearer, while the first needs a counterargument too.
The first is clearer, while the second still needs an example.
Both are equally clear, but the concession weakens each of them.
The first needs an example, while the second is already the strongest part.

feedback.es: En la nota, «the former argument is clearer than the latter» indica que el argumento citado antes es más claro y el citado después aún necesita un ejemplo.

origin.audio: Dear Sara, your piece is persuasive, and the ending is strong. Two small things: the former argument is clearer than the latter, which needs an example, and the phrase due to the fact that appears twice, so please tighten it up. As mentioned above, I would keep the concession, because it makes you sound fair. Best wishes, Carlos.

prompt.es: Completa: «Revisé mi borrador dos veces y recorté dos frases repetidas.»

feedback.es: Revised alude al trabajo de revisión documentada: releer y mejorar el borrador antes de entregarlo.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Una concesión prepara la respuesta en lugar de debilitar la tesis.»

answer.text: A concession prepares the answer rather than weakening the thesis
accepted: A concession prepares the answer rather than weakening the thesis
Rather than weakening the thesis a concession prepares the answer

feedback.es: Rather than contrapone lo que hace la concesión (preparar la respuesta) con lo que no hace (debilitar la tesis).
